    What's the next SpaceX launch date?
    An AI Overview is not available for this searchCan't generate an AI overview right now. Try again later.
    AI Overview
    SpaceX has frequent launches, but the next scheduled launch is a Starlink mission on a Falcon 9 rocket from Vandenberg SFB on Monday, March 16, 2026, around 7:37 PM PDT, followed by another Starlink mission from Cape Canaveral on March 17th. SpaceX aims for rapid, almost daily missions, primarily deploying more Starlink satellites using their reliable Falcon 9 rockets, with a major Starship test flight also anticipated in April 2026. 
    Key Upcoming SpaceX Launches:
    • March 16, 2026: Starlink Mission (Falcon 9) from Vandenberg SFB, California. 
    • March 17, 2026: Starlink Mission (Falcon 9) from Cape Canaveral, Florida. 
    • April 2026 (NET): Starship Flight 12 (Starship V3) from Starbase, Texas. 
    Where to Find Live Updates: 
    • SpaceX Official Site: SpaceX website.
    • Spaceflight Now: Spaceflight Now.
    • Space Launch Schedule: Space Launch Schedule.
    What to Expect:
    • Starlink Missions: The bulk of SpaceX's launches involve deploying batches of Starlink internet satellites. 
    • Falcon 9: Most missions use the Falcon 9 rocket. 
    • Starship: A significant test flight for the much larger Starship rocket is expected in April.

      Which Starship will launch next?
      An AI Overview is not available for this searchCan't generate an AI overview right now. Try again later.
      AI Overview
      SpaceX's next Starship launch, Integrated Flight Test 12 (IFT-12), is anticipated in late March or April 2026 from Starbase, Texas, featuring the new, more powerful Starship Version 3 (specifically Ship 39) and aiming for significant progress in booster and ship recovery. While previous launch windows in March 2026 were missed, the team is preparing Ship 39 for its debut, with potential for orbital attempts and ship catch experiments, but official dates are pending.
       
      Key Details for IFT-12: 
      • Vehicle: Starship Version 3 (Ship 39).
      • Location: Starbase, Texas.
      • Goals: Debut of V3, payload deployment, reentry experiments, booster return, and potential ship catch.
      • Timeline: Expected in late March or April 2026, though exact dates shift.
      What's Next After IFT-12?
      • Flight 13: Expected to be the first orbital flight with a tower catch attempt for the upper stage, but this depends on Flight 12's success. 
      • Florida Debut: A Starship launch from Florida is planned for late summer or fall 2026. 
      Stay updated via SpaceX's website, Wikipedia's Starship list, and Next Spaceflight for the most current launch schedules and news.

        • Date: October 13, 2025
        • Time: 6:23 p.m. CDT / 23:23 UTC
        • Location: Starbase, Texas (Pad 1)
        • Significance: Final flight for the Version 2 Starship/Super Heavy.
        For information on future launches, check the official SpaceX website or NASA's live stream page.

          What is the most powerful rocket ever built?
          An AI Overview is not available for this searchCan't generate an AI overview right now. Try again later.
          AI Overview
          The most powerful rocket ever built is SpaceX's Starship (fully stacked with its Super Heavy booster), generating over 29 million pounds of thrust, making it significantly more powerful than NASA's SLS and the historical Saturn V, though it's still in testing phases. NASA's SLS (Space Launch System) is the most powerful rocket currently flown operationally, while the Saturn V was the most powerful operational rocket before these new systems. 
          SpaceX Starship (Super Heavy Booster + Starship upper stage)
          • Thrust: Over 29 million pounds (combined). 
          • Key Feature: Designed for full reusability, aiming to drastically cut space travel costs. 
          • Status: Currently undergoing integrated test flights, with impressive power demonstrated but still developing full operational capabilities. 
          NASA Space Launch System (SLS)
          • Thrust: Around 8.8 million pounds (4 million kg). 
          • Key Feature: Backbone of NASA's Artemis program, designed to send humans to the Moon and beyond. 
          • Status: Has successfully flown, making it the most powerful rocket flown to date in operational status, but Starship is set to surpass it in power. 
          Historical Benchmark: Saturn V 
          • Thrust: About 7.5 million pounds.
          • Key Feature: The rocket that took astronauts to the Moon during the Apollo missions.
